chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Thal'abah, and he narrated to us from the one who mentioned him, from Maysara, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The oath upon which expiation becomes obligatory is that which was obligatory upon you to do, so you swore that you would not do it, and then you did it; so there is nothing upon you, because your deed is obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And that which was obligatory upon you not to do, so you swore that you would not do it, and then you did it; so upon you is the expiation.'
ai.seo_question: When does an oath require expiation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Transmitted through the chain of Thalabah and Maytharah, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential nuance that an oath to abstain from an obligatory act (wajib) does not incur expiation when fulfilled, as the action remains an act of obedience. Conversely, abstaining from a prohibited or recommended act requires expiation upon fulfillment, establishing a clear link between the nature of the act and the legal consequence of the oath. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that the validity of kaffarah depends on whether the sworn-off action is inherently obligatory or merely permissible/recommended.
